doctrines.conclusion_template: SOVEREIGN identity (Level 11.0) verification requires the full authentication ceremony protocol. No shortcut paths exist for the highest authority level. The Commander's identity must be established through multi-factor verification including knowledge challenge, behavioral pattern match, and bloodline position confirmation before any SOVEREIGN-level session can be created.
doctrines.reasoning_framework: The SOVEREIGN level represents absolute authority within the McWilliams Dynasty system. Unlike lower authority levels that may be verified through single-factor authentication, SOVEREIGN verification demands the complete ceremony protocol. This ensures that even in the event of credential compromise at lower factors, the highest privilege operations remain protected. The ceremony is a sequential multi-step process where each step must be completed before the next is revealed, preventing parallel attack vectors. The design principle is that convenience never supersedes security at the SOVEREIGN tier.
key_factors: Authorization phrase with full legal name
DOB verification as final sovereign confirmation
doctrines.burden_holder: System (must prove identity beyond reasonable doubt)
doctrines.adversary_position: Attacker may possess partial credentials from phishing or social engineering
counter_arguments: Ceremony adds friction to legitimate operations
Timeout may expire during complex verification
Knowledge challenges can be brute-forced given enough time
Behavioral patterns may shift over time
Device fingerprints can be cloned
doctrines.resolution_strategy: Multi-factor layering ensures no single compromised factor grants access. Ceremony timeout prevents slow brute-force. Failed attempt lockout prevents rapid retry. The combination of knowledge, position, and biometric factors creates a defense-in-depth architecture.

doctrines.conclusion_template: Multi-factor authentication in the Bloodline system uses three independent verification channels: knowledge (security question hash), behavioral (typing cadence and temporal patterns), and device (hardware fingerprint). Each factor contributes an independent confidence score, and their combination reduces composite fragility multiplicatively. A minimum of two factors should be verified for any operation above OPERATOR level.
doctrines.reasoning_framework: The MFA architecture follows the principle that authentication factors should be independent — compromise of one factor should not aid in compromising another. Knowledge factors are the most common but also the most phishable. Behavioral factors are harder to replicate but may drift over time as user patterns change. Device factors provide strong binding but can be circumvented by device cloning. The system assigns different confidence weights to each factor: knowledge (0.40), device (0.25), behavioral (0.20), with a base confidence of 0.10 for known identity. These weights reflect the relative strength and independence of each factor type.
key_factors: Knowledge: HMAC-SHA256 hashed security responses with pepper
Device: Hardware fingerprint matching against registered devices
Independence: Factors verified through separate channels
Composite fragility: multiplicative reduction across factors
doctrines.adversary_position: Attacker may possess one factor through theft, phishing, or surveillance
counter_arguments: MFA adds user friction and can cause lockouts
Behavioral biometrics have false positive rates
Device fingerprinting may fail on hardware changes
Knowledge factors remain vulnerable to social engineering
Factor synchronization across devices is complex
doctrines.resolution_strategy: Graduated authentication — lower-risk operations accept fewer factors, higher-risk operations require more. Failed factor attempts are tracked with exponential backoff lockout. New devices are accepted but with reduced confidence until pattern establishes.
doctrines.controlling_precedent: BLD01-DOCTRINE-002: Defense in Depth Through Factor Independence

doctrines.conclusion_template: Authority delegation allows the Commander (or any identity with delegate capability) to grant temporary, scoped access tokens to other identities. Delegations are strictly descending — a delegator can only grant levels below their own, up to the system maximum of 8.0 for delegates. All delegations have mandatory expiration times and can be revoked at any time by the delegator or any higher authority.
doctrines.reasoning_framework: The delegation framework implements the principle of least privilege with temporal bounds. Every delegation creates a new trust chain link that must be validated on each use. The system enforces that delegation chains are strictly descending — each link must be at a lower authority level than the previous. This prevents privilege escalation through chained delegations. Scope restrictions ensure that a delegate receives only the specific capabilities needed for their task, not blanket access. The maximum delegation level of 8.0 ensures that even the Commander cannot delegate SOVEREIGN or HEIR-level access, preserving the bloodline integrity.
key_factors: Revocable at any time by delegator or higher authority
Audit trail for all delegation actions
doctrines.burden_holder: Delegator (responsible for scope and duration appropriateness)
doctrines.adversary_position: Delegate may attempt to exceed granted scope or extend duration
counter_arguments: Delegation chains add complexity to authorization checks
Expired delegations may disrupt active operations
Scope definitions may be too coarse or too fine
Revocation propagation may have latency
Multiple active delegations create combinatorial permission sets
doctrines.resolution_strategy: Clear scope definitions with capability enumeration. Automatic expiration enforcement. Real-time revocation with session invalidation. Audit trail for forensic review of delegation usage.
doctrines.controlling_precedent: BLD01-DOCTRINE-003: Delegation is Privilege, Not Right

doctrines.conclusion_template: The succession protocol ensures continuity of the McWilliams Dynasty authority structure in the event of Commander incapacitation. A designated heir (maximum level 9.5) is pre-registered in the bloodline registry but remains dormant until activated by the dead man's switch. The succession chain is strictly ordered: SOVEREIGN -> HEIR APPARENT -> HEIR -> COMMANDER_DELEGATE. No heir can exceed level 9.5, preserving the uniqueness of SOVEREIGN authority.
doctrines.reasoning_framework: Succession planning addresses the single point of failure inherent in a SOVEREIGN-led authority structure. The dead man's switch monitors Commander heartbeats and triggers succession after a configurable timeout (default 72 hours). This timeout balances responsiveness against false positives from temporary unavailability. The heir is pre-registered but dormant — they cannot self-activate, preventing insider succession attacks. When activated, the heir gains their registered authority level (up to 9.5) but never SOVEREIGN (11.0). This design choice ensures that certain SOVEREIGN-only operations become permanently inaccessible until the Commander returns, creating a natural incentive for succession to be temporary.
key_factors: Dead man's switch with configurable timeout (default 72h)
Dormant until switch triggers — cannot self-activate
Ordered succession chain with no skip-levels
doctrines.burden_holder: Commander (must maintain heartbeat to prevent succession)
doctrines.adversary_position: Insider may attempt to suppress heartbeat to trigger false succession
counter_arguments: 72-hour timeout may be too long for critical operations
Heartbeat monitoring requires persistent infrastructure
Heir activation without Commander verification risks legitimacy
Multiple heirs create succession ambiguity
Network partition could prevent heartbeat delivery
doctrines.resolution_strategy: Configurable timeout allows Commander to set appropriate threshold. Heartbeat verification uses authenticated sessions. Single designated heir eliminates ambiguity. Network partition detection through multiple heartbeat channels.
doctrines.controlling_precedent: BLD01-DOCTRINE-004: SOVEREIGN is Unique and Non-Transferable

doctrines.conclusion_template: Emergency lockout is the nuclear option — it revokes ALL active sessions, ALL delegations, and ALL pending ceremonies in a single atomic operation. Only SOVEREIGN authority can trigger lockout. One emergency recovery session can be preserved to allow the Commander to lift the lockout when the threat is resolved. Global lockout blocks all new authentication attempts until lifted.
doctrines.reasoning_framework: The emergency lockout protocol is designed for worst-case scenarios: credential breach, insider attack, or system compromise. It prioritizes security over availability by immediately revoking all trust relationships. The preserved emergency recovery session is a careful compromise — without it, the Commander would be locked out of their own system. The recovery session is stored in a separate set and is the only session type that can lift the lockout. This creates a known, controlled recovery path while ensuring that any compromised sessions are immediately invalidated. The atomic nature of the operation ensures that partial lockout states cannot exist.
key_factors: Atomic: all sessions, delegations, ceremonies revoked simultaneously
Global lockout blocks all new authentication
Recovery requires the preserved emergency session
Full audit trail of lockout and recovery
doctrines.burden_holder: Commander (must verify threat before triggering lockout)
doctrines.adversary_position: Attacker with SOVEREIGN session could trigger lockout as denial-of-service
counter_arguments: Lockout disrupts all active operations
Recovery process introduces single point of failure
False positive lockout wastes time and trust
Emergency session itself could be compromised
No automated threat detection — relies on manual trigger
doctrines.resolution_strategy: Lockout is manual-only to prevent automated false positives. Recovery session uses highest-confidence authentication. All lockout events create permanent audit records. Post-lockout review process identifies root cause and prevents recurrence.
doctrines.controlling_precedent: BLD01-DOCTRINE-005: Emergency Lockout is Irreversible Except by Recovery

doctrines.conclusion_template: Sessions are time-bounded authentication tokens with a default TTL of 24 hours. Each session records the identity, authority level, authentication factors used, confidence score, and scope. Maximum concurrent sessions per identity is 5, preventing credential sharing. Sessions can be validated, revoked, or allowed to expire naturally. Expired sessions are automatically cleaned.
doctrines.reasoning_framework: Session management implements the principle that authentication state should be ephemeral and verifiable. Every session carries its own confidence score derived from the authentication factors used at creation time, meaning sessions created with fewer factors have reduced authority even for the same identity. The concurrent session limit of 5 prevents credential sharing while accommodating multiple devices. Session validation checks three conditions: existence, non-revocation, and non-expiration. The 24-hour TTL forces periodic re-authentication, limiting the window of exposure if a session token is compromised. Device fingerprint binding provides an additional layer of session integrity.
key_factors: Per-session confidence score from auth factors
Three validation checks: exists, not revoked, not expired
doctrines.burden_holder: System (must enforce TTL and concurrency limits)
doctrines.adversary_position: Attacker may attempt session fixation, hijacking, or token theft
counter_arguments: 24-hour TTL may be too long for high-security contexts
Session storage in memory is lost on restart
Concurrent limit may inconvenience legitimate multi-device users
Token-based sessions are bearer tokens (no proof of possession)
Session revocation has no push notification mechanism
doctrines.resolution_strategy: Configurable TTL for different authority levels. Session persistence to vault for restart recovery. Concurrent limit tunable per identity. Token binding to device fingerprint reduces bearer token risk.
doctrines.controlling_precedent: BLD01-DOCTRINE-006: Sessions are Ephemeral Trust Assertions

doctrines.conclusion_template: Behavioral pattern authentication uses hashed representations of user behavior (typing cadence, interaction timing) as an authentication factor. Unlike knowledge factors, behavioral patterns are difficult to transfer or steal because they represent subconscious physical characteristics. The system stores a baseline behavioral hash and compares new samples for consistency. Behavioral drift over time is expected and handled through gradual baseline updates.
doctrines.reasoning_framework: Behavioral biometrics represent the frontier of continuous authentication. Traditional authentication happens at a point in time (login), but behavioral patterns can provide ongoing confidence that the authenticated user is still the one operating the session. The hash-based comparison ensures that raw behavioral data is never stored — only a cryptographic representation. This protects user privacy while enabling verification. The confidence contribution of behavioral factors (0.20) is lower than knowledge (0.40) because behavioral patterns are probabilistic rather than deterministic. A new behavioral sample that differs from baseline may indicate either an impostor or natural drift — the system cannot distinguish these cases with certainty, hence the moderate confidence weight.
key_factors: Typing cadence as primary behavioral signal
Baseline drift handling through hash updates
doctrines.burden_holder: System (must distinguish legitimate drift from impostor)
doctrines.adversary_position: Sophisticated attacker may train to replicate behavioral patterns
counter_arguments: Behavioral patterns change with fatigue, stress, or injury
Hash comparison is binary — no partial match scoring
First-use registration creates a cold start problem
Environmental factors (keyboard, desk) affect typing cadence
Replay attacks could use recorded behavioral samples
doctrines.resolution_strategy: Behavioral is a supplementary factor, never sole. Hash updates accommodate natural drift. Replay prevention through temporal binding. Environmental normalization in future versions.
doctrines.controlling_precedent: BLD01-DOCTRINE-007: Behavioral Auth is Supplementary, Not Primary

doctrines.conclusion_template: Device trust is established through hardware fingerprint matching. Known devices receive higher confidence (0.25), new devices receive reduced confidence (0.15), and unknown devices from registered identities receive minimal confidence (0.05). First device registration is automatic during initial authentication. The device fingerprint list is maintained per identity and can grow as users add new trusted devices.
doctrines.reasoning_framework: Device fingerprinting binds authentication to specific hardware, creating a strong binding between identity and physical access. Unlike passwords or behavioral patterns, device fingerprints represent a 'something you have' factor. The graduated confidence model (known=0.25, new=0.15, unknown=0.05) reflects the decreasing trust as device familiarity decreases. Automatic first-device registration reduces friction for initial setup while maintaining security for subsequent authentications. The system stores fingerprints as opaque hashes — the actual hardware characteristics are never exposed, preventing fingerprint recreation attacks.
doctrines.burden_holder: User (must authenticate from registered or registerable devices)
doctrines.adversary_position: Attacker may clone device fingerprints or use stolen hardware
counter_arguments: Device fingerprints can be spoofed in software
Hardware replacement invalidates existing fingerprints
Multiple legitimate devices dilute device binding strength
VM environments produce unstable fingerprints
Privacy concerns with device tracking
doctrines.resolution_strategy: Device is one factor among several — spoofing alone is insufficient. Hardware replacement handled through re-registration with reduced initial confidence. VM detection adds risk flags.
doctrines.controlling_precedent: BLD01-DOCTRINE-008: Device Trust Enhances But Does Not Replace Identity

doctrines.conclusion_template: The authentication ceremony is a multi-step sequential verification process required for SOVEREIGN-level operations. It consists of 4-5 steps: identity confirmation, knowledge verification, bloodline position verification, sovereign action authorization, and (for SOVEREIGN level) final DOB confirmation. Each step must be completed in order within a 300-second timeout. A cryptographic challenge token rotates after each step to prevent replay attacks.
doctrines.reasoning_framework: The ceremony protocol is the highest-assurance authentication mechanism in the Bloodline system. It exists because single-factor or even multi-factor point-in-time authentication may not provide sufficient confidence for irreversible SOVEREIGN operations. The sequential nature of the ceremony ensures that each step builds on the confidence of the previous steps. The rotating challenge token prevents step-replay attacks where an attacker captures a valid step response and tries to use it later. The 300-second timeout is a carefully chosen balance: long enough for a legitimate user to complete all steps thoughtfully, short enough to prevent slow brute-force attacks on individual steps. Ceremony completion creates a session with the highest possible confidence score.
key_factors: Steps must be completed in prescribed order
Failed step records as auth failure (contributes to lockout)
Successful completion grants highest confidence session
doctrines.burden_holder: Authenticating party (must complete all steps within timeout)
doctrines.adversary_position: Attacker must compromise all ceremony steps within 5 minutes
counter_arguments: Ceremony is slow and inconvenient for frequent operations
Timeout may expire for users in high-latency environments
Sequential steps create a known attack surface
Challenge token rotation adds implementation complexity
Step verification logic must be kept secret
doctrines.resolution_strategy: Ceremony reserved for infrequent SOVEREIGN operations. Timeout is configurable. Each step uses different verification logic to prevent single-vector attacks. Token rotation prevents replay. Step logic is hashed, not cleartext.
doctrines.controlling_precedent: BLD01-DOCTRINE-009: Ceremony is the Gold Standard of Authentication

doctrines.conclusion_template: The system implements an automatic lockout after 5 failed authentication attempts within a 15-minute window. During lockout, all authentication requests for the affected identity are rejected. Lockout is per-identity, not global, to prevent denial-of-service against other identities. Failed ceremony steps count as failed attempts. The lockout window uses a sliding time window that automatically clears as old attempts age out.
doctrines.reasoning_framework: The lockout policy is the first line of defense against brute-force attacks. The threshold of 5 attempts in 15 minutes was chosen to accommodate legitimate typos (1-2 attempts) while quickly detecting systematic attacks. Per-identity lockout ensures that an attacker targeting one account cannot lock out the entire system. The sliding window approach (rather than fixed-window) prevents timing attacks where an attacker times their attempts to straddle window boundaries. Failed ceremony steps contribute to the lockout counter because ceremony attempts are authentication attempts — treating them differently would create an unprotected attack surface.
key_factors: Sliding time window for attempt tracking
Ceremony failures count as failed attempts
Automatic clearance as old attempts age out
doctrines.burden_holder: System (must accurately track and enforce limits)
doctrines.adversary_position: Attacker may use distributed sources or slow-rate attacks
counter_arguments: Lockout enables denial-of-service against specific identities
Legitimate users locked out by typos or changed passwords
Distributed attacks from multiple IPs bypass per-identity tracking
15-minute window may be too short for sophisticated attacks
No progressive lockout (5th attempt same as 50th)
doctrines.resolution_strategy: Per-identity scope limits DoS blast radius. SOVEREIGN lockout can only be triggered by the lockout endpoint, not by failed attempts. Future: progressive backoff and IP correlation.
doctrines.controlling_precedent: BLD01-DOCTRINE-010: Lockout Protects Against Brute Force

doctrines.conclusion_template: Every authentication decision carries a confidence stratification: DEFENSIBLE (>=0.90), AGGRESSIVE (>=0.75), DISCLOSURE (>=0.55), HIGH_RISK (>=0.30), or CEREMONY_REQUIRED (<0.30). The stratification determines what actions are permitted and what additional verification may be needed. Operations requiring SOVEREIGN authority always require DEFENSIBLE confidence, achievable only through full ceremony.
doctrines.reasoning_framework: Confidence stratification provides a framework for making nuanced authorization decisions rather than binary allow/deny. A session with AGGRESSIVE confidence may be permitted to perform routine operations but blocked from irreversible actions. This graduated approach reduces friction for low-risk operations while maintaining high assurance for critical ones. The thresholds were calibrated based on the multi-factor confidence weights: a user providing all three factors (knowledge=0.40 + device=0.25 + behavioral=0.20 + base=0.10 = 0.95) achieves DEFENSIBLE. Two factors typically achieve AGGRESSIVE. One factor typically achieves DISCLOSURE.
key_factors: Five stratification levels with clear thresholds
doctrines.burden_holder: System (must accurately compute and enforce confidence levels)
doctrines.adversary_position: Attacker may attempt to manipulate confidence scores through factor injection
counter_arguments: Threshold values are somewhat arbitrary
Confidence computation is additive, not probabilistic
Intermediate levels create ambiguous authorization states
Users may not understand why operations are blocked
Confidence decay over session lifetime not implemented
doctrines.resolution_strategy: Thresholds calibrated to multi-factor weight sums. Clear action guidance per level. User-facing error messages explain required additional factors. Future: time-decay confidence model.

doctrines.conclusion_template: The bloodline chain represents the authority lineage of the McWilliams Dynasty. The chain is strictly ordered: PATRIARCH (SOVEREIGN, 11.0) -> FIRST_IN_LINE (HEIR_APPARENT, 9.5) -> additional heirs (HEIR, 9.0). Each position in the chain has a fixed maximum authority level that cannot be exceeded. The chain is immutable once established — positions can only be modified by the SOVEREIGN through authenticated ceremony.
doctrines.reasoning_framework: The bloodline chain is the foundational trust anchor of the entire authentication system. Unlike delegation (which is temporary and scoped), bloodline positions are permanent authority grants tied to dynastic succession. The strict ordering ensures unambiguous authority resolution — there is never a question of who has higher authority in any dispute. The immutability requirement (modification only through ceremony) prevents unauthorized manipulation of the succession chain. The PATRIARCH position at level 11.0 is unique by design — no other position can reach this level, ensuring that the Commander always has ultimate override authority.
doctrines.burden_holder: SOVEREIGN (sole authority to modify bloodline chain)
doctrines.adversary_position: Insider may attempt to elevate their bloodline position
counter_arguments: Rigid hierarchy may not adapt to changing circumstances
Single SOVEREIGN creates critical dependency
No mechanism for SOVEREIGN removal if compromised
Bloodline metaphor may not map to organizational needs
Chain length is limited by authority level granularity
doctrines.resolution_strategy: Dead man's switch provides continuity mechanism. Ceremony requirement prevents unauthorized modification. Authority level granularity (0.1 increments) allows fine-grained chain ordering.
doctrines.controlling_precedent: BLD01-DOCTRINE-012: Bloodline Authority is Inherited, Not Earned

doctrines.conclusion_template: Every authentication event is logged to an append-only JSONL audit trail with SHA-256 integrity hashes. The audit trail records authentication attempts (success/failure), session operations, delegations, ceremonies, lockouts, and dead man's switch events. Each entry includes a unique ID, timestamp, event type, and data payload. The integrity hash ensures tamper detection.
doctrines.reasoning_framework: The audit trail serves two purposes: operational monitoring and forensic investigation. The append-only design prevents log modification — entries can only be added, never changed or deleted. Each entry's SHA-256 hash is computed over the entry's canonical JSON representation, creating a verifiable chain of integrity. The JSONL format enables efficient streaming reads and is compatible with standard log analysis tools. The comprehensive event coverage ensures that any authentication-related action can be reconstructed from the audit trail, supporting both real-time monitoring and post-incident forensics.
key_factors: Covers all auth events: authenticate, delegate, ceremony, lockout, heartbeat
Queryable by event type with limit control
doctrines.burden_holder: System (must ensure log integrity and completeness)
doctrines.adversary_position: Attacker may attempt to delete or modify logs to cover tracks
counter_arguments: Append-only log grows unboundedly
Local storage is vulnerable to disk failure
Hash chain can be recomputed if entire log is compromised
High-volume systems may have logging performance impact
Sensitive data in logs creates privacy considerations
doctrines.resolution_strategy: Log rotation with compression. Cloud backup to R2. Hash verification on periodic integrity checks. Sensitive data masking in log entries. Performance-optimized async logging.
doctrines.controlling_precedent: BLD01-DOCTRINE-013: Every Auth Action Leaves a Permanent Record

doctrines.conclusion_template: All secrets in the Bloodline Authenticator are stored as HMAC-SHA256 hashes with a system pepper. Raw secrets are never stored, logged, or transmitted. The HMAC key and pepper are loaded from environment variables, defaulting to built-in values for development. Constant-time comparison (hmac.compare_digest) is used for all hash comparisons to prevent timing attacks. Token generation uses cryptographically secure random sources (secrets module).
doctrines.reasoning_framework: Cryptographic secret handling follows defense-in-depth principles. HMAC-SHA256 (rather than plain SHA-256) ensures that even if an attacker obtains the hash database, they cannot verify candidate secrets without the HMAC key. The pepper adds a second layer — even with the HMAC key, the pepper must also be known. Constant-time comparison prevents timing side-channel attacks where an attacker measures response time to determine how many bytes of a hash matched. The secrets module provides OS-level entropy for token generation, ensuring unpredictability. All of these measures collectively ensure that the secret storage is robust against known cryptographic attack vectors.
key_factors: Raw secrets never stored or logged
doctrines.burden_holder: System (must protect secrets at all stages)
doctrines.adversary_position: Attacker may attempt hash extraction, timing attacks, or rainbow tables
counter_arguments: HMAC-SHA256 is fast — not ideal for password hashing (vs bcrypt/argon2)
Default HMAC key and pepper reduce security in development
Key rotation requires re-hashing all stored secrets
Single pepper means all hashes compromised if pepper leaks
No salt per-secret means identical secrets produce identical hashes
doctrines.resolution_strategy: Production deployments must set unique environment variables. Future: migrate to Argon2id with per-secret salt. Key rotation protocol with graceful migration. Secret uniqueness enforced at registration time.
doctrines.controlling_precedent: BLD01-DOCTRINE-014: Secrets are Write-Only — Hash In, Never Out

doctrines.conclusion_template: The Bloodline Authenticator's threat model considers five primary attack vectors: credential theft (phishing, keylogging), session hijacking (token theft, network interception), insider threat (heir/delegate misuse), brute force (systematic credential guessing), and social engineering (impersonation). Each vector is mitigated by specific countermeasures: MFA against credential theft, device binding against session hijacking, authority limits against insider threat, lockout against brute force, and ceremony against social engineering.
doctrines.reasoning_framework: Threat modeling is the foundation of security architecture. Rather than defending against every possible attack, the system focuses on the most likely and most impactful threats. Credential theft is the most common attack vector and is mitigated by requiring multiple independent factors. Session hijacking is addressed by binding sessions to device fingerprints and implementing short TTLs. Insider threats are controlled by strict authority limits and audit trails. Brute force is prevented by attempt lockout. Social engineering — the most sophisticated attack — is countered by the ceremony protocol, which requires knowledge that cannot be obtained through manipulation alone (DOB, bloodline position). The defense-in-depth approach means that no single countermeasure failure is catastrophic.
doctrines.burden_holder: System (must implement and maintain all countermeasures)
doctrines.adversary_position: Sophisticated attacker may combine multiple vectors (multi-stage attack)
counter_arguments: Threat model may not cover novel attack vectors
Countermeasures add complexity that can introduce new vulnerabilities
Advanced persistent threats may operate below detection thresholds
Physical access attacks are not fully addressed
Supply chain attacks on dependencies are out of scope
doctrines.resolution_strategy: Regular threat model reviews. Drift watcher detects anomalous patterns. Audit trail supports post-incident analysis. Ceremony protocol is the last line of defense for highest-value operations.
doctrines.controlling_precedent: BLD01-DOCTRINE-015: Defense in Depth — No Single Point of Failure

doctrines.conclusion_template: Every authentication decision in the Bloodline Authenticator includes a SHA-256 determinism hash computed over the canonical JSON representation of the decision inputs. Given identical inputs (identity, factors, timestamps), the system produces identical hashes, enabling external verification that authentication decisions are consistent and reproducible. This is critical for audit compliance and dispute resolution.
doctrines.reasoning_framework: Determinism in authentication decisions means that the same inputs always produce the same outputs. This property is essential for audit verification — an auditor can replay a recorded authentication attempt and verify that the system would have made the same decision. The SHA-256 hash serves as a compact proof of determinism: if the hash matches, the decision was consistent with the recorded inputs. The canonical JSON serialization (sorted keys, minimal separators) ensures that formatting differences don't affect the hash. This approach transforms authentication from a trust-me system to a verify-me system.
key_factors: Minimal separators to eliminate formatting variance
Hash included in every authentication response
Enables external verification and audit replay
Consistent across system restarts and versions
doctrines.adversary_position: Attacker may attempt to manipulate inputs to produce desired hash
counter_arguments: Determinism requires excluding non-deterministic inputs (timestamps, random IDs)
Hash collision risk (theoretical, negligible for SHA-256)
Version changes may alter canonicalization
Floating-point inputs may not be deterministic across platforms
Hash verification requires access to all original inputs
doctrines.resolution_strategy: Determinism hash excludes timestamps and random tokens. SHA-256 collision resistance is sufficient for audit purposes. Version field in hash inputs detects version-related changes.
doctrines.controlling_precedent: BLD01-DOCTRINE-016: Every Decision is Verifiably Reproducible
